title: "Reproducibility exercise: git and pixi"
format:
  html:
    code-overflow: wrap
---

In this exercise, you will turn the molecular clock analysis from Capstone
Project 2 into a ***reproducible project***: one that anyone (including you,
a year from now) can download and rerun with a single command, using exactly
the same software, and get exactly the same results.
Along the way, you will:

1.  Use ***git*** to keep track of every change to your project, and
    ***GitHub*** to back it up
2.  Use ***pixi*** to create a ***project environment*** with
    all the software needed for the project, including:
    
    -   Python
    -   Python packages
    -   [IQ-TREE](https://iqtree.github.io/), the program I used to estimate
        the tree of 24 SARS-CoV-2 genomes in Capstone Project 2

3.  Estimate that tree yourself, fit the molecular clock to it, and record
    every step, so that the whole analysis can be rerun with one command
4.  Prove that your project is reproducible by deleting your project and
    rebuilding everything from your GitHub repository

There is no new Python or biology in this exercise.
Everything new is about ***how*** we do the work.

The exercise has five parts.
Each part takes about 30 minutes, and each one ends with saving your
work to GitHub, so you can stop at the end of any part and pick up where you
left off later.
Put your answers to the questions into the Exercise 13 quiz on Canvas.

::: {.callout-important}
## Save your work to GitHub at the end of every part

Your GitHub codespace is ***temporary***.
It stops on its own after 30 minutes of inactivity, and GitHub ***deletes***
codespaces that haven't been used for 30 days, ***even if they contain work
you haven't pushed to GitHub***.
Your work is only safe once you have committed it and pushed it to GitHub
(you'll learn how in Part 1).
:::

## Part 1: Your project repository

### Make your copy and open your codespace

1.  Go to the
    [Comp Bio project template](https://github.com/phyletica/comp-bio-project-template)
    on GitHub, and follow the instructions in its README under the following
    two sections **ONLY**:

    -   ***"Make your own copy of this repository"***:
        Name your repository `comp-bio-project`, and choose ***Public***
    -   ***"Open your codespace"***: When you get a "Do you trust the authors
        of the files in this folder?" pop-up, click "Trust Folder & Continue"

    Stop and come back here once you get to ***"Set up your project environment"***
    (don't set up the environment; we will do that below)

2.  Once your codespace is ready, you should see your files on the left side
    of VS Code and a ***terminal*** at the bottom.
    Click in the terminal and check that you're in your project's folder:

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    pwd
    ls -a
    ```

    `pwd` (**p**rint **w**orking **d**irectory) tells you what directory
    ("folder") you are in, which should be `/workspaces/comp-bio-project`.
    This folder you are in is called your ***working directory***.
    `ls -a` lists all files and directories in your working directory. When you
    run this command, you should see `README.md` and a folder named
    `.devcontainer` (plus a folder named `.git`; more on that below).

The terminal is the same Bash command line you used in the
[Bash exercise](bash-exercise.qmd), running on a Linux computer in the cloud.
All of the commands in this exercise are typed in the terminal.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Copying commands

Hover over any code block on this page and click the clipboard icon in its
upper right corner to copy it.
To paste into the terminal, use **Ctrl + Shift + V** (or right-click and
choose "Paste").
:::

### What is a git repository?

Your project folder is a ***git repository***.
That means git is keeping a history of the folder in the hidden `.git`
folder.
(Never edit or delete the `.git` folder!)
The history is a series of ***commits***: snapshots of your files, each with
a message describing what changed, who changed it, and when.
Your repository on GitHub is a copy of the same history.

Making a commit takes three steps:

1.  **Change** some files (*e.g.*, edit them, create them, or delete them)
2.  **Stage** the changes you want to include in the next commit, with
    `git add`
3.  **Commit** the staged changes, with `git commit`, which saves the snapshot
    in your repository's history

Then, `git push` sends your new commits to your copy of the repo on GitHub.

### Your first commit

1.  Let's see what git thinks of our repository right now by running these two
    commands in the terminal:

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    git status
    git log
    ```

    `git status` should say `nothing to commit, working tree clean`, which
    means none of your files have changed since the last commit.
    `git log` lists the commits in your repository's history (just one so far,
    which GitHub made when you copied the template).

    ::: {.callout-note}
    ## Leaving `git log` (and `git diff`)
    When the output of a git command is longer than your terminal, git shows
    it one page at a time.
    Use the arrow keys to scroll, and press **q** to quit and get back to the
    command line.
    :::

2.  In the file list on the left of VS Code, click `README.md` to open it.
    At the very top of the file, add these lines (with your name), and
    leave a blank line between them and the rest of the file
    (**note**: To add the text below to the `README.md` file, you will edit it
    using the top window of VS Code, not the terminal):

    ```{.markdown filename="README.md"}
    # Dating the ancestor of SARS-CoV-2

    Author: Your Name

    A reproducible molecular clock analysis of 24
    SARS-CoV-2 genomes, for BIOL 5/6800.
    ```

    VS Code saves automatically after a moment (or press **Ctrl + S**).

3.  Now, return to the terminal window, and ask git again:

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    git status
    ```

    **Note**: You will need the output from this command for Question 2 below.

4.  Add your change to git's staging area. This prepares it for the next
    commit:

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    git add README.md
    ```

    Ask git for the status again:

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    git status
    ```

    **Note**: You will need the output from `git status` for Question 2 below.

5.  Commit your change to git's database, with a message that says what you
    changed:

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    git commit -m "Adding project title and author to README"
    ```

    Now, when you run:

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    git log
    ```

    you should see two commits, with yours at the top.
    The long string of letters and numbers next to each commit is its
    ***hash***: a unique ID for that snapshot.

6.  Send your commit to GitHub:

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    git push
    ```

    Go to your repository's page on GitHub (`github.com/your-username/comp-bio-project`)
    and refresh it.
    Your README should show your changes, and near the top of the file list,
    you should see your commit message.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Always use `-m` with `git commit`
If you forget the `-m "message"` part, git opens a text editor in the
terminal and waits for you to type a message there.
If that happens, the easiest way out is to close the editor: If the bottom of
the terminal shows `^X Exit`, press **Ctrl + X**; if it shows a lot of `~`
characters, type `:q!` and press Enter.
Then run the `git commit` command again with `-m`.
:::

### Questions

**Question 1**: Paste the URL of your GitHub repository (*e.g.*,
`https://github.com/your-username/comp-bio-project`).

**Question 2**: What did `git status` say about `README.md` (a) after you
edited it, but before `git add`, and (b) after `git add`, but before
`git commit`?

## Part 2: A reproducible environment

Just like any computer, your codespace already has software that 
came with the codespace's operating system.
Someone else's computer (or this codespace, next year) will have different
versions of software, with different packages installed, or none at all.
If our analysis depends on "whatever is installed on this computer," we can't
expect it to give the same results anywhere else.

To get around this problem, we will use ***pixi*** to create a ***project
environment***: a folder of software that belongs to this project, with every
package's version written down so that the environment can be rebuilt exactly,
anywhere.

### Create the environment

1.  Tell pixi to start managing an environment for this project:

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    pixi init
    ```

    Then, ask git to show you the status of things:

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    git status
    ```

    `pixi init` created three files:

    -   `pixi.toml`: the ***manifest***, which lists what our project needs
    -   `.gitignore`: a list of files and folders that git should ignore
    -   `.gitattributes`: settings that tell git how to treat certain files

    Click `pixi.toml` in VS Code to open it.
    It doesn't list any software yet; the `[dependencies]` section is empty.

2.  Return to the terminal window and add Python and the Python packages we
    need using the following command:

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    pixi add "python=3.14.*" numpy scipy matplotlib
    ```

    This takes a minute or two.
    pixi figures out a set of package versions that work together (*e.g.*,
    which versions of NumPy work with Python 3.14), downloads them from
    [conda-forge](https://conda-forge.org/) (a large, free collection of
    scientific software), and installs them into a hidden folder named
    `.pixi` in your project.

    The `"python=3.14.*"` part asks for Python version 3.14 (any 3.14.x
    release), instead of whatever version is newest on the day you run the
    command, which might not be compatible with your project's code or
    the packages it depends on.

3.  Look at `pixi.toml` again.
    The `[dependencies]` section now lists each package with a range of
    versions (something like `numpy = ">=2.3.5,<3"`).
    There is also a new file, `pixi.lock`, the ***lock file***.
    Open it and scroll through it (it's long!).
    It lists the ***exact*** version of every package that pixi installed,
    including the packages that our packages need, and the address it was
    downloaded from.

    -   The manifest (`pixi.toml`) says what we ***asked for***
    -   The lock file (`pixi.lock`) says exactly what we ***got***

    When pixi builds the environment from a lock file, it installs exactly
    those versions.

4.  Confirm the version of Python pixi installed in our environment:

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    pixi run python --version
    pixi list
    ```

    `pixi run` runs a command ***inside*** the project environment.
    `pixi list` lists every package in the environment, and its version (pixi
    installed **a lot** of packages that the packages we requested depend on!).

### Commit the environment

1.  Check what has changed:

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    git status
    ```

    Notice that the `.pixi` folder, which holds the installed software, is
    ***not*** listed.
    Look in `.gitignore` to see why.
    We never commit the installed software, only the instructions for
    rebuilding it (`pixi.toml` and `pixi.lock`).

2.  Prepare (stage) the four new files for the next commit:

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    git add pixi.toml pixi.lock .gitignore .gitattributes
    ```

    Then, commit the new files to the git database:

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    git commit -m "Creating a pixi environment with Python 3.14"
    ```

    Lastly, use `git push` to back up your project database to GitHub:

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    git push
    ```

### Add a program that isn't Python

IQ-TREE is written in C++, not Python, so you can't install it with Python's
usual tools (and it doesn't work in molab).
But it is available from [bioconda](https://bioconda.github.io/), a
collection of bioinformatics software that works with pixi.

1.  Tell pixi to look for software in bioconda (after conda-forge):

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    pixi workspace channel add bioconda
    ```

    Then, add IQ-TREE:

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    pixi add iqtree
    ```

    Check to see which version of IQ-TREE pixi installed:

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    pixi run iqtree3 --version
    ```

2.  See what changed, using `git diff`, which shows exactly which lines
    changed in each file since the last commit:

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    git status
    git diff pixi.toml
    git diff --stat
    ```

    In `git diff`, lines that start with `-` (in red) were removed, and lines
    that start with `+` (in green) were added.
    `git diff --stat` summarizes how much each file changed.
    (`pixi.lock` shows up as `Bin` because the `.gitattributes` file tells git
    not to bother showing line-by-line changes for it; it's written by pixi,
    not by people.)

3.  Prepare the changes to `pixi.toml` and `pixi.lock` for the next commit:

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    git add pixi.toml pixi.lock
    ```

    Commit the changes and push them to GitHub:

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    git commit -m "Adding IQ-TREE from bioconda"
    git push
    ```

### Questions

**Question 3**: What version of Python did `pixi run python --version` report?

**Question 4**: What range of versions does `pixi.toml` list for `numpy`?
What exact version of NumPy is in your environment (look for it in
`pixi list`)?
Why is it useful to have both?

**Question 5**: What version of IQ-TREE is in your environment (look for
`iqtree` in `pixi list`)?
Write it down; you will need it in Part 5.

**Question 6**: Why doesn't git list the `.pixi` folder in `git status`, and
why don't we want to commit it?

## Part 3: Estimating the tree with IQ-TREE

To make an analysis reproducible, we need to record not only the software,
but also the ***steps***: the exact commands we ran, in order.
pixi can store commands in `pixi.toml` as ***tasks***, which anyone can run
with `pixi run <task name>`.

### Get the data

1.  Add a task that downloads the alignment of 24 SARS-CoV-2 genomes we've
    been using (it's one long command; use the copy button!):

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    pixi task add get-data "mkdir -p data && curl -L -o data/sars-cov-2.fasta https://raw.githubusercontent.com/phyletica/intro-to-comp-bio/refs/heads/main/notebooks/data/SARS-CoV-2.nextclade.aligned.fasta" --description "Download the SARS-CoV-2 alignment"
    ```

    Look at the new `[tasks]` section of `pixi.toml` to see the task.
    The `-p` option tells `mkdir` not to complain if the `data` folder already
    exists, so the task still works if we run it again.

2.  Now, run the task:

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    pixi run get-data
    ```

    Check that it worked:

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    grep ">" data/sars-cov-2.fasta
    ```

    You should see the names of the 24 genomes.

3.  The alignment is small (about 700 KB), so we will commit a copy of it.
    That way, our project still works even if the file at that web address
    changes or disappears, and the task records where the data came from.

    Stage the new task (in `pixi.toml`) and the data file for the next commit
    (`git add`), and then commit them to git's database:

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    git add pixi.toml data/sars-cov-2.fasta
    git commit -m "Adding task to download the SARS-CoV-2 alignment, and the data"
    ```

::: {.callout-note}
## What about big data?
GitHub doesn't allow files larger than 100 MB, and repositories should stay
under a few GB.
For big data sets, we would commit only the task that downloads the data
from a permanent public archive (like GenBank), and tell git to ignore the
data files.
:::

### Run IQ-TREE

1.  Add a task that runs IQ-TREE on the alignment:

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    pixi task add tree "mkdir -p results && iqtree3 -s data/sars-cov-2.fasta -m HKY -seed 1 -T 1 --prefix results/tree --redo" --description "Estimate a maximum likelihood tree with IQ-TREE"
    ```

    Here's what each part of the IQ-TREE command does:

    | Option | What it does |
    |:--|:--|
    | `-s data/sars-cov-2.fasta` | The alignment to analyze |
    | `-m HKY` | Use the HKY model of sequence evolution (as in Capstone Project 2) |
    | `-seed 1` | The ***seed*** of IQ-TREE's random number generator (more on this in Part 4) |
    | `-T 1` | Use one processor (the results can differ slightly with more) |
    | `--prefix results/tree` | Begin all output files with the prefix `results/tree.*` |
    | `--redo` | Overwrite the output files if they already exist |

2.  Run it:

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    pixi run tree
    ```

    IQ-TREE prints a lot as it searches for the maximum likelihood tree, but it
    only takes a few seconds.
    Near the end, look for the `BEST SCORE FOUND`: the log-likelihood of the
    best tree it found.

3.  See what IQ-TREE created:

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    ls results
    git status
    ```

### Decide what to commit

IQ-TREE writes several files.
The one we need is `results/tree.treefile`, which has the tree in Newick
format (click it in VS Code to take a look).
The others are reports, logs, and temporary files that IQ-TREE can recreate
in a few seconds.
Open `results/tree.log` and look at its first few lines: it records the date
and time IQ-TREE ran, so it changes ***every*** time we run IQ-TREE, even
when the results are exactly the same.
It's not worth cluttering our git database with these trivial changes.

We'll tell git to ignore IQ-TREE's other files.

1.  Open `.gitignore` in VS Code, and add these lines to the end of the file:

    ```{.default filename=".gitignore"}
    # IQ-TREE files that we can recreate, and that change every time IQ-TREE runs
    results/*.log
    results/*.iqtree
    results/*.ckp.gz
    results/*.bionj
    results/*.mldist
    ```

    Each line is a ***pattern***, where `*` means "anything."
    For example, `results/*.log` matches every file in `results` whose name
    ends with `.log`.
    Lines that start with `#` are comments.

2.  Check that git now ignores those files (only `results/tree.treefile`
    should be listed in the `results` folder):

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    git status --untracked-files=all
    ```

3.  Stage the changes to `.gitignore` and `pixi.toml` and the tree estimated by
    IQ-TREE:

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    git add .gitignore pixi.toml results/tree.treefile
    ```

    Commit the changes in git's staging area to the database:

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    git commit -m "Estimating the ML tree with IQ-TREE"
    ```

    And sync your updated database with the copy on GitHub:

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    git push
    ```

### Questions

**Question 7**: What was the log-likelihood of the best tree IQ-TREE found
(the `BEST SCORE FOUND`)?

**Question 8**: Why is it a good idea to tell git to ignore files like
`results/tree.log`?

## Part 4: Fitting the clock, and using your project's history

### Add the analysis script

1.  Make a new `scripts` directory ("folder"):

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    mkdir scripts
    ```

    Download the `clock.py` script that fits the molecular clock into the
    `scripts` directory:

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    curl -L -o scripts/clock.py https://raw.githubusercontent.com/phyletica/intro-to-comp-bio/refs/heads/main/scripts/clock.py
    ```

    Open `scripts/clock.py` in VS Code and skim it.
    It's the same code we used in Capstone Project 2, as a plain Python
    script instead of a notebook: It reads IQ-TREE's tree, calculates each
    genome's distance from the root, fits the clock, prints the results, and
    saves a plot to `results/clock.png`.

2.  Now, try running the `clock.py` Python script:

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    pixi run python scripts/clock.py
    ```

    When it finishes, click `results/clock.png` in VS Code to view the plot the
    script created.

3.  Add a task for it.
    The `--depends-on tree` part tells pixi that this task needs the `tree`
    task to run first:

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    pixi task add clock "python scripts/clock.py" --depends-on tree --description "Fit a molecular clock to the tree"
    ```

    You can verify that pixi added the task using:

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    pixi task list
    ```

    Now, run the new `clock` task:

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    pixi run clock
    ```

    One command, `pixi run clock`, runs the **whole analysis**, from
    estimating the tree to creating the plot.
    Nice!

4.  Add the script, the plot it created, and the changes to `pixi.toml` to
    git's staging area:

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    git add pixi.toml scripts/clock.py results/clock.png
    ```

    Commit the staged changes to the database, and push the new commit to
    GitHub:

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    git commit -m "Adding the molecular clock script and task"
    git push
    ```

### Change the analysis

In Capstone Project 2, we found that Omicron doesn't follow the clock.
Let's change the analysis to leave Omicron out, and use git to see and record
the change.

1.  Open the `scripts/clock.py` file in the VS Code window, find this line
    (it's about 40 lines from the bottom of the file):

    ```{.python filename="scripts/clock.py"}
    excluded_lineages = []
    ```

    and change it to:

    ```{.python filename="scripts/clock.py"}
    excluded_lineages = ["Omicron"]
    ```

2.  Rerun the analysis:

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    pixi run clock
    ```

    When it finishes, see what has changed with:

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    git status
    ```

    and:

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    git diff scripts/clock.py
    ```


    `git status` lists `results/clock.png` and `scripts/clock.py` as changed,
    but not `results/tree.treefile`.
    IQ-TREE ran again, but because we used the same data, software, and seed,
    it produced exactly the same tree file, so git sees no change.

3.  Look at the new plot, then add the changes to the staging area, commit, and
    push:

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    git add scripts/clock.py results/clock.png
    git commit -m "Leaving Omicron out of the clock"
    git push
    ```

### Go back in time

Git keeps every version of every file you've committed, so you can always
look at (or go back to) an earlier version.

1.  List your commits, one per line:

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    git log --oneline
    ```

    `HEAD` is git's name for your latest commit, and `HEAD~1` means "one
    commit before `HEAD`."

2.  To bring back the plot from the commit before your latest one,
    use the `git restore` command:

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    git restore --source=HEAD~1 results/clock.png
    ```

    and ask git for the status:

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    git status
    ```

    Look at the `results/clock.png` plot in VS Code (it should include Omicron
    again).

3.  Put the latest version back:

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    git restore results/clock.png
    ```

    and ask git for the status:

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    git status
    ```

    Now, when you look at `results/clock.png` in VS Code, it should be the
    version that excludes Omicron.

    `git restore <file>`, without `--source`, throws away any changes to the
    file since your last commit.
    This is also how you undo a mistake: if you break a file, you can always
    get back the last version you committed.

### Why the seed matters

IQ-TREE uses random numbers while it searches for the best tree.
The seed determines which random numbers it gets: the same seed gives the
same random numbers, and so the same results.
(If you don't give IQ-TREE a seed, it picks one based on the current time.)
Let's see what happens with a different seed.

1.  In `pixi.toml`, in the `tree` task, change `-seed 1` to `-seed 2`.
    Then, run the analysis again:

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    pixi run clock
    ```

    Compare the results to what it printed before (the rate, the date of the
    ancestor, and $R^2$).

    Use git to see what changed:

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    git status
    ```

    and:


    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    git diff --color-words='[^,():]+' results/tree.treefile
    ```

    The `--color-words` option shows the changes word by word (here, each
    name and branch length is a "word"), instead of line by line.
    The old values are in red and the new values are in green.

2.  Undo the change to the seed, and the results it produced:

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    git restore pixi.toml results/
    ```

    And confirm everything is restored to match your last commit:

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    git status
    ```

### Questions

**Question 9**: With Omicron left out, what rate (substitutions per genome
per year) and date of the ancestor did the clock estimate?
(They should be close to what you found in Capstone Project 2.)

**Question 10**: When you changed the seed to 2, what changed in
`results/tree.treefile`?
Did the clock's printed results change?
Do you think the tree from seed 2 is a different scientific result than the
tree from seed 1?
Why is it still important to record the seed?

## Part 5: Prove it's reproducible

So far, everything has been on one computer: your codespace.
The real test of reproducibility is whether the project works on a ***new***
computer.
So, let's delete your codespace, make a brand new one, and rebuild
everything from your GitHub repository.

1.  First, make sure all of your work is on GitHub.
    `git status` should say `nothing to commit, working tree clean`, and
    `Your branch is up to date with 'origin/main'`:

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    git status
    ```

    If not, commit and push before you go on!
    Anything that isn't pushed will be lost when you delete the codespace.

2.  Go to <https://github.com/codespaces>, click the **"..."** next to your
    codespace, and choose **"Delete."**

3.  Go to your repository on GitHub, and create a new codespace
    (**"Code"** → **"Codespaces"** → **"Create codespace on main"**).
    While it starts up, it will automatically run `pixi install`, which
    rebuilds your environment from `pixi.toml` and `pixi.lock`.

4.  In the new codespace, check your environment:

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    pixi list
    ```

    Rerun the whole analysis:

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    pixi run clock
    ```

    And check to see if anything changed:

    ```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
    git status
    ```

If `git status` says `nothing to commit, working tree clean`, then you just
reproduced your entire analysis, on a new computer, from scratch, and got
***exactly*** the same tree and the same plot, down to the last byte.

::: {.callout-note}
## What if git says a file changed?
IQ-TREE sometimes uses slightly different (but equally correct) arithmetic
on different kinds of processors, so on a different computer the branch
lengths in `results/tree.treefile` might differ in their last digits.
If git says that the tree file changed, look at the changes with
`git diff --color-words='[^,():]+' results/tree.treefile` to see how big they
are, and then use `git restore results/` to go back to your committed results.
:::

## Optional: Reproduce a classmate's analysis

Anyone can rebuild and rerun a public project.
Ask a classmate for their repository's URL, and try it in your codespace
(replace `their-username` below with their GitHub username):

```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
cd /tmp
git clone https://github.com/their-username/comp-bio-project
cd comp-bio-project
pixi run clock
git status
cd /workspaces/comp-bio-project
```

`git clone` downloads a copy of a repository, including its whole history.
Did you get exactly their results?

## Quick reference

| Command | What it does |
|:--|:--|
| `git status` | Show which files have changed since your last commit |
| `git add <file>` | Stage a file's changes for your next commit |
| `git commit -m "message"` | Save a snapshot of the staged changes, with a message |
| `git push` | Send your commits to GitHub |
| `git log --oneline` | List your commits, newest first |
| `git diff <file>` | Show what changed in a file since your last commit |
| `git restore <file>` | Throw away a file's changes since your last commit |
| `git restore --source=HEAD~1 <file>` | Bring back a file as it was one commit ago |
| `git clone <URL>` | Download a copy of a repository |
| `pixi init` | Start a pixi project (creates `pixi.toml`) |
| `pixi workspace channel add <channel>` | Add a channel (like bioconda) for pixi to search for packages |
| `pixi add <package>` | Add a package to the environment (updates `pixi.toml` and `pixi.lock`) |
| `pixi list` | List the packages in the environment, and their versions |
| `pixi run <command>` | Run a command inside the environment |
| `pixi task add <name> "<command>"` | Save a command as a task in `pixi.toml` |
| `pixi task list` | List the tasks in `pixi.toml` |
| `pixi run <task>` | Run a task |
| `pixi install` | Rebuild the environment from `pixi.toml` and `pixi.lock` |
